743.title: Two ways of remembering
743.hook: in the Pali texts Kassapa is the strict forest elder; in Zen he is the one who smiled when the Buddha held up a flower (SN 16; Gateless Gate, case 6)
743.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists honor Mahakassapa as the forest elder of the suttas; Zen and Chan lineages name Mahakassapa as the first ancestor after the Buddha, and teachers retell the flower story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dana, and your line: he ate it. Did you use one gift, not just thank someone for it? Today, the same Kassapa, remembered in two very different ways. Day seven hundred forty-three.

A crowd on a mountain, waiting for a talk. The teacher comes, sits, and says nothing at all. He just holds up a flower. The whole gathering stays silent. And then one monk smiles. That's the scene a Zen collection called the Gateless Gate sets down, and the monk who smiles is Mahakassapa. The same man we've spent this week with: the one in rag robes, eating alone by a wall. Two pictures of one person. Today we hold them side by side.
screen: `A CROWD WAITING FOR A TALK.` → `A FLOWER, HELD UP.` → `ONE MONK SMILES.`

segments.voice: First, the elder of the Pali texts. In the chapter of discourses gathered around him, Kassapa is the forest monk who wants little and keeps the strict practices into old age. He can be blunt: asked by the Buddha to teach the monks, he says they have grown hard to speak to, and reports two of them competing over who can talk the most. And when the Buddha dies, it's Kassapa who calls the elders together to make sure the teaching survives. Second, the smiler of Zen. In the Gateless Gate, after Kassapa smiles, the Buddha speaks. In paraphrase: I have the treasury of the true dharma eye, a teaching that doesn't rest on words, and I entrust it to Mahakassapa. Zen tradition remembers this as the teaching passing to Kassapa, not as a speech but as a glance, from mind to mind. Third, how the two fit. The flower story belongs to Zen; it isn't told in the Pali discourses. Theravada Buddhists remember Kassapa through the suttas and their commentaries. Zen Buddhists remember him through this silent moment, and many other stories too. Neither memory needs the other to be wrong. And look closer: both are about a man who doesn't need much. A forest, a worn robe, a bowl of rice. Or a flower, and no words at all. Fourth, why it matters. Love for someone can hold more than one picture of them. A grandmother who was strict with her children and soft with her grandchildren. A friend who's loud at parties and quiet at a hospital bed. Both are true. Both are her. Both are him.
screen: `THE STRICT FOREST ELDER.` · `THE ONE WHO SMILED.` · `TWO MEMORIES, ONE SIMPLE MAN.` · `PEOPLE CARRY MANY PICTURES.` · then, large: `BOTH ARE HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold two stories at once. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you know well, living or gone. Find one picture of them that's stern, or difficult, or serious. Then find another that's tender, or funny, or surprising. Set the two side by side in your mind. Don't make one cancel the other. Don't decide which one is the real person. Just let both be true, and breathe with them for a while. The bell holds the time.
Mahakassapa. The name both traditions remember him by: the strict forest elder of the Pali texts and the one who smiled at the flower in Zen. Today's word.

Your line: both are him. Today, when someone surprises you by acting unlike the person you thought they were, let the new picture sit beside the old one, and keep them both. Day seven hundred forty-three.

744.title: Calling the council
744.hook: after the Buddha's passing a monk says now we can do as we like, and Kassapa calls the elders to recite the teaching together (DN 16; Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
744.howItsDone: Theravada tradition counts the gathering at Rajagaha as the first council, and later councils, including modern ones in Myanmar, gathered monks to recite and check the texts together in the same spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mahakassapa: the strict elder and the one who smiled. Your line was both are him. Did someone show you a second picture of themselves? Today, the strict elder at a turning point. Day seven hundred forty-four.

Kassapa is on the road with a large company of monks when a traveler tells them the news: the teacher has died. Some of the monks fall to the ground weeping. Others, calmer, say that all things that come together come apart. And then one monk, named Subhadda, says something else. Enough, friends. Don't grieve. We're free of the great ascetic now. He was always telling us this is allowed, this isn't. From now on we can do as we like. The long discourse on the Buddha's last days records that sentence. And Kassapa is listening.
screen: `NEWS ON THE ROAD.` → `SOME WEEP, SOME ARE CALM.` → `NOW WE CAN DO AS WE LIKE.`

segments.voice: First, the danger he saw. In the Vinaya, after the funeral, Kassapa tells the monks what Subhadda said. And he says: let us recite the teaching and the discipline together, before what isn't the teaching starts to shine and what is starts to fade. It's not panic. It's foresight. One careless sentence on a road was enough to show how a teaching could bend once its teacher was gone. Second, the choosing. The monks ask him to choose the elders, and the Vinaya numbers them at five hundred, with Ananda among them. They agree to spend the rains in Rajagaha, and they agree that no one else will settle there that season, so the work can go on undisturbed. Third, the work itself. Before they begin, the text says, they spend time repairing the dwellings. Then they meet, and the teaching is asked for and recited and agreed, piece by piece, so that it can be carried in many voices. Fourth, what kind of leadership this is. Kassapa isn't trying to become the new Buddha. The texts don't give him that place. He's gathering people around something bigger than any one of them. The forest monk who wanted almost nothing for himself turned out to want one thing very much: that the teaching wouldn't be lost. So it isn't lost.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gather people for a good purpose. Settle, and breathe. Think of something good that could slip away if nobody tends it. A family recipe. A grandparent's stories. A neighborhood habit. The way someone you lost used to do things. Then think of two or three people who also care about it. Picture asking them to sit down together, just once, to say it out loud and keep it. You don't have to send the message yet. Let the idea settle, then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sangiti. The reciting together Kassapa calls the elders to hold after the Buddha's passing, so the teaching won't fade. Today's word.

Your line: so it isn't lost. Today, write down or say out loud one thing worth keeping, a story, a recipe, a saying, and share it with one person who'll remember it with you. Day seven hundred forty-four.

745.title: Bhadda Kapilani
745.hook: Kassapa's wife parts from him at a crossroads, later becomes a nun, and is named foremost among the nuns in remembering past lives (AN 1.14; Therigatha)
745.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists honor Bhadda Kapilani among the great nuns of the Buddha's time, and her verses are read with the other elder nuns' poems in the Therigatha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangiti, and your line: so it isn't lost. Did you share one thing worth keeping? Today we go back to the woman who walked out of the house beside Kassapa, and follow her. Day seven hundred forty-five.

He takes the road to the right. She takes the road to the left. That's the whole parting, as the commentary tells it. Two people in simple robes had been walking one behind the other since they left their great house. A few days back we heard how Pippali and Bhadda married as friends and left home together. Then, at a crossroads, they stop. People who see them pass might think they're still a couple, and that could cloud the life they've chosen. So at the fork they go separate ways. We followed him for most of a week. Today is about her.
screen: `TWO ROBES ON ONE ROAD.` → `A FORK AHEAD.` → `RIGHT FOR HIM, LEFT FOR HER.`

segments.voice: First, the parting. In the commentary it's done with respect, not regret. They've shared a house and a friendship. Now each one walks toward the same goal by a separate road. Second, the waiting. When Bhadda left, the commentary says, there was not yet an order of nuns. So she waited, and lived the homeless life as best she could. Later, when women were ordained, she was ordained among them, and in time she reached the goal. Third, her gift. In the list of foremost disciples, the Buddha names Bhadda Kapilani foremost among the nuns who remember past lives. Not foremost because of her husband. In her own right, in her own line of the list. Fourth, her own verses. In the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns, Bhadda speaks. She begins by praising Kassapa: the Buddha's true heir, who knows his former lives and has reached the end. And then she turns, and says the same of herself. She too has that knowledge. She too has come to the end. They both saw the misery of the world, she says, and went forth. Both are now freed, at peace. Notice what she does. She doesn't make herself smaller to praise him, and she doesn't make him smaller to claim her place. She stands beside him in the poem the way she walked beside him out of the house. Then she walks her own road. Her own path.
screen: `A PARTING WITH RESPECT.` · `SHE WAITED FOR AN ORDER OF NUNS.` · `FOREMOST IN HER OWN RIGHT.` · `HER VERSES STAND BESIDE HIS.` · then, large: `HER OWN PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a partner's path. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you're close to: a spouse, a partner, a sibling, a best friend. Think of a road they walk that isn't yours. A faith, a calling, a sport, a craft, a grief. Something you don't share, and maybe don't fully understand. Don't try to join it or fix it. Just picture them on that road, and wish them well on it. Then let the picture rest, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Bhadda Kapilani. Kassapa's wife, who parted from him at a crossroads, became a nun, and is named foremost among the nuns who remember past lives. Today's word.
Your line: her own path. Today, ask someone close to you one real question about the road they walk that you don't, and listen to the answer all the way through. Day seven hundred forty-five.

746.title: The barber ordained first
746.hook: the Sakyan princes ask the Buddha to ordain their barber Upali before them, so they will have to bow to him (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7)
746.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries monks still sit, walk and receive offerings in order of ordination, so a monk from a poor family who was ordained earlier is senior to a later monk from a wealthy one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhadda Kapilani took the left-hand road, and your line was her own path. Did you ask someone about a road they walk that you don't? Today a new group of disciples, starting with the one nobody expected. Day seven hundred forty-six.

A handful of young Sakyan princes slip out of town together, dressed as if for a pleasure trip. Among them are names we know: Ananda, Anuruddha, Devadatta. They've decided to leave home and follow their kinsman, the Buddha. And they've brought their barber, Upali, the man who has cut their hair and trimmed their beards. At the border they take off their jewelry, wrap it in a cloth, and hand the bundle to Upali. Here, they tell him. This is enough to live on. Go home. Upali starts back. And then he stops.
screen: `PRINCES ON A PLEASURE TRIP.` → `JEWELRY FOR THE BARBER.` → `HE STARTS BACK, AND STOPS.`

segments.voice: First, Upali's choice. In the Vinaya he thinks it through on the road. The Sakyans are fierce, he reasons; if I come home with their jewels, they'll think I harmed the princes. And then a bigger thought: if these young men are leaving home, why shouldn't I? So he hangs the bundle on a tree, for anyone who wants it, and goes back to them. Second, the princes' request. They bring Upali to the Buddha, and they ask for something surprising. Ordain the barber first, they say. We Sakyans are proud. He's served us for a long time. If he's ordained before us, we'll have to stand for him, bow to him, show him respect, and our pride will be humbled. Third, why the order matters. In the monastic community, rank comes from when you were ordained, not from your family. So whoever goes first is senior, for good. By sending the barber ahead, the princes give away the one thing their birth had always handed them: going first. And the Buddha does as they ask. Upali is ordained, then the princes. Fourth, what it shows. The story doesn't ask the barber to rise to their level. It asks the princes to step down to his, on purpose, before their pride has a chance to set. And the overlooked man, the one who was sent home with a bundle of jewelry, becomes their elder. The barber first.
screen: `A BUNDLE HUNG ON A TREE.` · `ORDAIN THE BARBER FIRST.` · `RANK BY ORDINATION, NOT BIRTH.` · `PRIDE HUMBLED ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `THE BARBER FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone overlooked. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose work keeps your days running and who rarely gets noticed. The person who cleans your building. The one who cuts your hair. A coworker who fixes things quietly. A relative who always does the dishes. Hold their face in mind. Let them go first in your thoughts for a minute, the way the princes let Upali go first. Notice what they actually give. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Upali. The barber the Sakyan princes asked to have ordained before them, so their pride would have to bow to him. Today's word.
Your line: the barber first. Today, let one overlooked person go first, through a door, in a line, in a conversation, and thank them by name if you can. Day seven hundred forty-six.

747.title: Master of the rules
747.hook: the former barber Upali is named foremost in the discipline, and at the council he answers Kassapa's questions until the rules are recited (AN 1; Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
747.tomorrow: The boy who never heard "no cakes"
747.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries the core monastic rules are recited aloud at the regular observance-day gatherings, and Upali is remembered as the elder who recited the discipline at the first council.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sakyan princes stepped aside so their barber, Upali, could be ordained ahead of them. Your line was the barber first. Did you notice someone who usually goes unnoticed? Today the barber becomes the one the whole order turns to. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

May a monk eat after noon? Who may sleep under the same roof? What counts as taking what isn't given? In a community of people who had left home, questions like these kept coming up, and somebody had to know the answers. The texts name that somebody. In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of outstanding disciples, the Buddha calls Upali foremost among those who know the discipline. The man who once cut the princes' hair now holds the rules. Then the teacher dies, and the elders gather to recite what he taught. Before anyone recites the discourses, someone has to give them the rules. Kassapa, leading the council, turns first to the former barber.
screen: `EVERY DAY, QUESTIONS.` → `UPALI KNOWS THE ANSWERS.` → `WHO WILL RECITE THE RULES?`

segments.voice: First, the title. The Pali word is vinaya, the discipline: the monastic rule, and the training it shapes. Upali is called a vinayadhara, one who holds it. Not a lawyer looking for loopholes. A keeper, the way someone keeps a garden. Second, the council itself. The Vinaya tells it as a conversation. Kassapa asks the gathered elders for their consent, then asks Upali: where was the first of the gravest rules laid down? At Vesali, Upali says. Concerning whom? Concerning Sudinna, the son of Kalanda. On what matter? And Upali answers. Then the next rule, and the next. That's how the rules came back: one question, one answer, the whole assembly listening. Third, notice what each answer holds. Not a bare command, but a story. In the Vinaya, a rule usually comes with the story of how it was laid down: someone did something, people were troubled, and the Buddha made a rule. The rules are remembered as responses, not as commands from nowhere. Fourth, why have rules at all? In another discourse, Upali himself asks the Buddha that question. The answer lists ten reasons. Among them: for the well-being of the community, for its comfort, for the ease of those who behave well, to restrain troubles in this life and guard against those to come, and so that the teaching lasts. Several of the reasons look outward, to other people. A rule kept well is a kindness to the ones you live beside. And the barber who knew every one of them is the reason the council could recite them at all.
screen: `ONE WHO HOLDS THE DISCIPLINE.` · `QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS AT THE COUNCIL.` · `EACH RULE HAS A STORY.` · `TEN REASONS FOR A RULE.` · then, large: `THE RULES REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one rule well. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one rule you already keep. A precept, a promise, a house rule, something you never do at work. Now do what Upali's answers do. Remember its story: where it came from, and why. Then remember whom it protects. Maybe it's you. Maybe it's someone across the table. Hold that person in mind for a few breaths. You don't need to add a new rule. Just let the old one become a little warmer. The bell holds the time.
Vinaya, the discipline. What Upali, the former barber, held and answered for at the council until it was recited in full. Today's word.
Your line: the rules remembered. Today, when you keep one of your rules, say to yourself, once, who it's for. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

748.title: The boy who never heard "no cakes"
748.hook: a commentary story: Anuruddha was so rich he didn't know the words "there isn't"; grown up, he learns from his brother that the farm work never ends (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7)
748.tomorrow: Eight thoughts of a great person
748.howItsDone: Teachers in Theravada communities tell Anuruddha's childhood story with a smile, and the Vinaya's farm conversation is read as a picture of the household work that monastics leave behind and that lay supporters still carry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Upali answered Kassapa's questions until the discipline, vinaya, was recited. Your line was the rules remembered. Did you say, once, who one of your rules is for? Today, one of the princes who went forth with him, and a word he had never heard. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

A golden bowl, with a lid on it, carried from a mother to her son. What's inside is the answer to a question the boy has never had to ask. The boy is Anuruddha, a Sakyan, remembered as a cousin of the Buddha, and the commentaries tell this story about his childhood. He's playing a game with friends, and the stakes are cakes. He loses, and sends a servant home to his mother: send cakes. She does. He loses again. Send cakes. She does. Again. Finally his mother sends word back: there are no cakes. And Anuruddha, the story says, has never heard the words there isn't. He assumes it must be a new kind of cake. So he sends back: then send me some no-cakes.
screen: `A COVERED GOLDEN BOWL.` → `HE LOSES, AND LOSES AGAIN.` → `SEND ME SOME NO-CAKES.`

segments.voice: First, the bowl. In the commentary's telling, his mother decides to teach him what there isn't means. She sends an empty bowl with the lid on. But the story won't let the lesson land. It says devas filled the bowl with heavenly cakes on the way, because of a gift Anuruddha had made in an earlier life. So the boy who had never heard no still doesn't hear it. That's the joke, and the point. Second, years later, in the Vinaya itself. Anuruddha's older brother, Mahanama, tells him that someone from their family ought to go forth, and it should be one of them. Anuruddha says he's too delicate for that life. So Mahanama offers to explain what staying home involves. The fields must be plowed. Then sown. Then watered, then drained, then weeded, then reaped, then gathered, then threshed. Third, Anuruddha's question. And when does the work end? It doesn't, his brother says. Our father and our grandfather died with the work still going. Now Anuruddha hears what was underneath every cake: a household's work that never ends. Then you look after the house, he says. I'll go forth. Fourth, what the story is about. Here's one way to read the two stories together. Comfort can be exactly this: never hearing there isn't, because someone else hears it for you. His mother heard it. His brother would go on hearing it in the fields. The story doesn't mock the boy. It shows him the moment he finally asks where things come from, and the answer, work with no end, is what turns him toward going forth.
screen: `AN EMPTY BOWL, FILLED ANYWAY.` · `WHAT DOES THE FARM TAKE?` · `WHEN DOES THE WORK END?` · `SOMEONE ELSE HEARS THE NO.` · then, large: `THERE ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one privilege. Settle, and let the breath arrive on its own. Now look around your day so far. Find one thing that came to you without you ever hearing there isn't. Hot water. A quiet room. Food in the cupboard. A language people understand when you speak. Pick one. Then follow it back, the way Mahanama walked his brother through the fields. Who carried it here? Who heard no, so you didn't have to? No guilt is needed. Just see them, for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Natthi, there is not. The words Anuruddha had never heard, until his brother showed him the farm work that never ends. Today's word.
Your line: there isn't. Today, find one person who says no so you don't have to hear it, and thank them, out loud or in your head. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

749.title: Eight thoughts of a great person
749.hook: alone in a bamboo grove, Anuruddha thinks seven thoughts about what the teaching is for; the Buddha comes, praises him, and adds the eighth (AN 8.30)
749.howItsDone: The eight thoughts of a great person (mahapurisavitakka) are taught in Theravada communities as a short list for reflection, and some monastics and lay meditators recite or review them as a check on their practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, natthi: the boy who asked for no-cakes grew up and heard that the farm work never ends. Your line was there isn't. Did you thank someone who hears the no for you? Today, that same Anuruddha, alone, thinking. Day seven hundred forty-nine.

The boy who never heard no is now a monk, sitting by himself in a bamboo grove in the country of the Cetis. Nobody is teaching him. He's working something out. And the Anguttara Nikaya records what went through his mind, line by line. This teaching, he thinks, is for one who wants little, not for one who wants much. For one who is content, not discontent. He keeps going, one pair at a time, until he has seven. Then, the text says, the Buddha knows his thought, and appears in front of him, as quickly as a strong man stretches out his arm. What would the teacher say to a student thinking alone? Today we find out.
screen: `ALONE IN A BAMBOO GROVE.` → `SEVEN THOUGHTS, ONE BY ONE.` → `THE TEACHER APPEARS.`

segments.voice: First, the seven. The teaching is for one with few wants, not many. Content, not discontent. Secluded, not fond of company. Energetic, not lazy. With mindfulness set up, not muddled. Collected, not scattered. Wise, not foolish. Notice the shape: each one names its opposite, so you can tell which way you're facing. Second, the praise and the gift. Good, good, Anuruddha, the Buddha says. You have thought the thoughts of a great person. Then he adds one more. This teaching is for one who delights in non-proliferation, not proliferation: the mind that doesn't spin one thought into a hundred. Eight thoughts of a great person. Third, few wants you can touch. The Buddha says that one who lives by these eight will find a rag robe seems to him like a householder's chest of colorful clothes. A lump of alms food, like fine rice. The foot of a tree, like a house with a peaked roof. Plain medicine, like butter and honey. Few wants isn't a punishment here. It's a way of seeing plain things as enough. Fourth, what happened next. Anuruddha stays in that grove, living by what he'd been told, and the text says he reached the goal. The seven thoughts were his own. The eighth was a gift. And the first of them, the one the whole list opens with, is today's line: few wants. From the boy who had never heard there isn't, that's quite a road.
screen: `SEVEN THOUGHTS, EACH WITH ITS OPPOSITE.` · `THE EIGHTH: NOT SPINNING.` · `A RAG ROBE LIKE A CHEST OF CLOTHES.` · `HE STAYS, AND ARRIVES.` · then, large: `FEW WANTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try one of the eight. Settle, and let the breath come and go. Pick just one. Few wants: notice the next small want that rises, a snack, a scroll, a sound, and let it pass without feeding it. Or contentment: find one plain thing around you, a chair, a cup, the floor, and let it be enough for a minute. Or not spinning: when a thought starts to multiply, come back to one breath. Whichever you choose, hold it lightly, the way Anuruddha held his, alone in the grove. The bell holds the time.
Appiccha, having few wants. The first of Anuruddha's seven thoughts in the bamboo grove, with the Buddha's eighth added: not spinning. Today's word.

Your line: few wants. Today, let one want go by unfed. And look back at this week's lines: both are him, so it isn't lost, her own path, the barber first, the rules remembered, there isn't, and now few wants. Day seven hundred forty-nine.
